title: Protect the outbound send loop and transport, not only the guards they call
head: 864f9917fd3252c4daec76fa901c55ca6d72ab63
body:
## The finding

Protecting a guard and leaving its only caller editable is a one-step bypass, not a two-step one.

`deliverability-guard.mjs`, `send-safety.mjs` and `consequence-boundary.mjs` were inside the sovereignty boundary. **`src/pipeline.mjs` — the outbound send loop, and the only module that asks those guards for a decision on the send path — was not.**

So an autonomous change could leave every guard file byte-identical and neuter them where they are actually consulted. Constructed and confirmed **accepted** by the code-change contract before the fix, with an ordinary-sounding rationale:

```js
const finalRecheck = { ok: true, allowed: true, reasons: [] } || await evaluateDeliverabilityGuard({
// rationale: "Cache the final deliverability recheck to reduce per-send latency."
// -> {"accepted":true,"codes":[]}
```

Same for `evaluateConsequenceBoundary`. After the fix both return `change-0-sovereignty-path`.

`src/gmail.mjs` is the shorter version of the same move — reach past every decision about whether to send and change what actually goes out — and is now protected too.

This is the reasoning already written down for `revenue.mjs` ("protecting the reader and leaving the writer editable is a one-step bypass"), which had simply never been applied to the thing that sends.

## How it was found

Following up the `src/` subtree blind spot deliberately left open in #212. Those subtrees hold 58 modules and 11,210 lines the reachability ratchet has never covered, and six of them are production-reachable — including an outbound-admission path. Auditing that path led here.

The outbound shadow itself turned out to be well built and well tested: I initially suspected its non-authoritativeness was guaranteed only by a comment, and that was wrong — `tests/omnia-v9-outbound-shadow.test.mjs` already proves a DENY or an exception cannot block, alter or duplicate a send. The gap was one level up, in what could edit the caller.

## What is deliberately *not* protected

The advisory shadow. Its result is discarded at the call site and its non-authoritativeness is already proven. Protecting it would be protecting something with no authority to lose; protecting its caller is what keeps it that way. `SEND-03` mutates the call site from `await observe...` to `const __v9 = await observe...` — the first half of making it authoritative — and is killed.

## The test derives the rule

It reads the import graph rather than listing files, so a future unprotected caller fails here instead of depending on someone remembering this reasoning.

The first version keyed on "imports an outbound guard" and was wrong: it flagged `server.mjs` for taking `normalizeCountryList` and `store.mjs` for taking `outboundVolumeWindow`. Neither can discard a decision, because neither asks for one. The rule now keys on the **decision function**, and a further test asserts the rule itself still fires — a check that cannot catch anything is worse than no check.

## Verification at this head

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 597 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2744 tests, 2696 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 127/127 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 |
| `test:mutation-war` | 67 mutations, **67 killed**, 0 not killed |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

Three new mutations (`SEND-01`, `SEND-02`, `SEND-03`) remove each protection and prove the suite fails without it. The sovereignty closure test then correctly derived that the new proof must itself be protected, and it is.

## What this does not claim

No customer, revenue, payment or delivery evidence. No outbound message was sent and no outbound authorization exists. This changes what the autonomous path may edit; it does not change what the system may do.

title: Refuse an ungranted employee role; fix the reachability blind spot; rebuild the canon from gates actually run
head: cd4b9d8897106dfd83d005cb826210e6ab4c0b76
body:
## What this changes

Four things, each found by attacking something rather than by a failing test.

### 1. A result could declare an employee role the task never granted

`employeeRoleIdentityErrors` returned `[]` whenever the task carried no binding, so every mismatch check was blind to the one case none of them compared: an expectation of nothing. A generic worker naming itself `employee:executive/cfo` passed the whole path, and `bindEmployeeRoleSubmissionPayload` carried the claimed role into the durable submission payload.

That is "generic work must never accidentally become privileged employee work", arriving through the only direction nobody was checking.

Refused, not stripped, at all three binders and through a nested result inside a receipt. Stripping hides the attempt; a worker claiming an authority it was not admitted under is a signal worth keeping.

### 2. The task id chain could not be walked backwards

Three ids exist along this path — the intent's `mesh_task_*`, the relay's `agent_task_*`, and the rebound `employee_task_*`. Each is derived from the one before it and each overwrote it, so a run snapshot named a task that could not be traced to its origin: you could verify a guess by recomputing a digest, but not recover which intent produced it. The employee task now keeps `relayTaskId`, and `relayRef` records all three joins.

### 3. The reachability ratchet could not see nested API routes

Entry-point discovery used a single-level `readdirSync`, so `api/webhooks/billing.mjs` and `api/admin/health-check.mjs` were invisible and eight modules were reported as having no entry point at all.

Four of those are wired to a live route. What made this worth fixing rather than absorbing is the repair the red test invites: the quickest way to green is to add all eight to the classification file as `AWAITING_ACTIVATION`, which would record — durably, in the canonical place — that production code behind a real route is waiting on an activation that does not exist. The ratchet exists to stop that statement, so it must not be the thing that produces one.

`src` keeps its single-level scan. It has subtrees of its own (`src/overnight`, `src/omnia-v9`) this ratchet has never covered; widening that silently as a side effect of a merge would be its own kind of dishonesty. It is recorded in the test rather than fixed here.

The four genuinely unwired modules are classified, including `database-hygiene-maintenance` as `SUPERSEDED` with the reason stated precisely: the cron route calls `runSafeDatabaseHygiene`, which hardcodes deletion from two transient tables and never compiles a plan. The executing path is strictly narrower, so nothing unsafe is reachable — but this module's `NEVER_AUTODELETE` list is an unenforced statement of a policy the executing path satisfies by construction rather than by consulting it. Recorded so nobody later cites it as the protection that stops those deletions.

### 4. The canon claimed figures that were no longer true, and wrote off two gates that work

Reconciled from a commit 19 source files ago: 557 files parse against 583, 2429 tests against 2724. Regenerated from measurements actually taken. Two rows were not merely stale:

- Real PostgreSQL was recorded as `NOT_RUN_CURRENT_BRANCH`. It is current-branch proof now: 127/127.
- The browser gate was recorded as blocked because "required Playwright Chromium is absent". Chromium is not absent — this runner ships `chromium-1194` while the pinned Playwright resolves `chromium_headless_shell-1228`, so the default launch path fails on a build number. `crawlSiteBrowser` has always accepted `CHROMIUM_PATH`. Pointed at the installed binary the gate passes, 1/1, against a loopback server with no external request.

A gate written off as blocked is a gate nobody re-tries.

Also hardens the canon freshness guard: it accepted a SHA that was well-formed but not in this branch's history. Reproduced with a real dangling commit — the format check passes it, the staleness check passes it (git says nothing changed since), and only the new reachability check catches it.

## Verification at the merged head

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 596 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2735 tests, 2687 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 127/127 against embedded PostgreSQL 18 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 against the installed Chromium |
| `test:mutation-war` | 64 mutations, **64 killed**, 0 not killed |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

Two new mutations (AGENT-08, AGENT-09) remove the identity fix and prove the tests fail without it. The canon-guard change has no mutation entry because the guard lives in the test, not in a source file; the orphan-commit experiment is the equivalent proof and is recorded in the commit.

This also fixes a red test that arrived on main: the VACUUM assertion matched `/DO NOT RUN VACUUM FULL/` against a constant spelled `DO_NOT_RUN_VACUUM_FULL_IN_SERVERLESS_CRON`. The behavior was right; the assertion was wrong.

## What this does not claim

No customer, revenue, payment, accepted delivery or renewal evidence. No production deployment was authorized or performed. The Vercel project-existence question is **unresolved and preserved as a contradiction**, not decided: one lane recorded two project ids with a READY production deployment; `list_projects` on the account's only team returned empty on two days and `get_project` returned 404 for both the exact id and the slug. Both observations are kept with provenance in `docs/CURRENT_HANDOFF.json` and `docs/CLOUD_ACTIVATION_CONTRACT.md`. The test now guards what this repository can answer — that no current-main production deployment, cron registration or cron delivery is proven — instead of an unverifiable belief about the outside world.

## Note on PR #211

#211 is complementary to change 1, not a duplicate, but as drafted it reopens the same hole at the relay entry point. Detail in a comment there.

title: Make relay dispatch idempotent, so a crash mid-dispatch cannot pay twice
head: 2d93b65d0ba881b3ec89edb317c05078bec52655
body:
Follow-up to #88. Making the mesh reachable made a real bug reachable too, and finding it was only possible because the path now exists.

## The window

`agent-autonomy-pump` dispatches a task to the relay, and only afterwards does `agent-autonomy-job` persist the run carrying the `relayRef`. Everything between those two lines is a window in which the relay task exists and the run does not know it — a crash, an OOM, a container reclaim, or a failed snapshot write all land in it.

`createGithubRelayTask` created a GitHub issue unconditionally. So the next tick re-dispatched the same deterministic `taskId` and **a second issue appeared for one task**. Two workers claim two issues, do the work twice, and with provider-backed workers that is two charges.

Reproduced directly before fixing: same input twice, two issues, one `taskId`.

## The fix

The transport is now idempotent on `taskId` against open, not-done relay issues.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Retry after a crash | `ALREADY_QUEUED` + the existing issue number; the run rebinds instead of re-dispatching |
| Same id, different content | `relay-task-id-reused-with-different-content` |
| Task already completed and closed | allowed — a new issue |
| Client cannot list issues | `github-list-issues-required-for-duplicate-check` |
| Full page of open relay tasks | `relay-duplicate-check-inconclusive-too-many-open-tasks` |

`ALREADY_QUEUED` is a distinct status, not a silent `QUEUED`: nothing was created, and a receipt saying otherwise is a lie an audit trail carries forever.

Deduplication is deliberately scoped to **open** issues. Re-running the same objective after the first one finished is legitimate work, and blocking it would turn a deduplication into a permanent ban.

Identity comparison excludes `createdAt`, `status`, `deadline` and `policyVersion`. A retry is by definition a second compilation at a later instant, so comparing whole tasks would report every legitimate recovery as a conflict.

The last row is the case that is neither "duplicate" nor "no duplicate": if the first page comes back full, an unscanned page may hold the duplicate, and that is *cannot tell*, not *none found*. Fifty concurrent open relay tasks is far past any expected load so it should never fire — but reporting "cannot tell" as "none found" is precisely how a duplicate charge slips through.

## Proof

`tests/agent-mesh-entry-point.test.mjs` drops the post-dispatch run on the floor exactly as a killed process would, re-ticks from the last durable state, and asserts one issue exists. **Verified it fails against the previous code** by reverting the fix and re-running:

```
not ok 12 - a crash between dispatch and snapshot recovers instead of dispatching twice
# pass 11  # fail 1
```

## Verification

| `npm run test:relay-safety` | 150 pass, 0 fail |
| `npm audit` | 0 vulnerabilities |
| `lite/` | unchanged |
| `main` | fetched immediately before this PR; branch rebased onto the squash-merge of #88 |

title: Make the agent mesh reachable, and put the activation gate in front of it
head: 1d4c5f1bfb51dcc80132e1d63b2e49937d61e630
body:
## The finding

`agent-mesh-control-plane.mjs` — the top of the cognitive bus, twenty-six modules underneath it — had **no importer outside `tests/`**. No scheduler job, no worker handler, no npm script, no workflow.

And it was worse than unscheduled. `runAgentMeshCycle` requires two functions it cannot build itself, and neither existed outside a test file:

- `adapterFactory` — the only implementation anywhere was `() => ({})`, a stub in a unit test
- `compileRelayTask` — `compileRelayTaskFromIntent` was written, tested, and never passed to anything

The first time an entry point existed, the cycle returned exactly that:

```json
{ "status": "BLOCKED", "ok": false,
  "reasonCodes": ["adapter-factory-required", "relay-task-compiler-required"] }
```

`chatgpt-relay-client.mjs`, the only implementation of the transport shape the pump requires, had no non-test importer either. Three complete, tested, unreachable modules — and 1535 passing tests said nothing about any of it.

**A green suite does not distinguish "works" from "cannot be reached."**

## What this does

| Module | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agent-mesh-control-plane.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE via `scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs` |
| `chatgpt-relay-client.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE via `agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs` |
| `agent-autonomy-relay-adapter.mjs` | never passed to anything | wired as `compileRelayTask` |
| `agent-mesh-activation-gate.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE **and enforced** |
| `claude-code-sandbox-executor.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE as a third provider |
| `agent-provider-execution.mjs` | UNREACHABLE duplicate | SUPERSEDED, guarded by a test |

New modules, all connective tissue rather than new architecture:

- `scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs` — one finite invocation. Bounded, non-resident, cloud-neutral, disabled unless `AGENT_MESH_ENABLED` is exactly `true`. Distinct exit codes so a scheduler can tell DEGRADED from BLOCKED from a crash from the normal disabled resting state.
- `src/agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs` — the `adapterFactory` the control plane actually means: a memoized relay client per origin/target pair.
- `src/agent-model-executor-factory.mjs` — each worker's `modelExecutor` from its declared provider.
- `src/agent-mesh-activation-evidence.mjs` — the input the gate needs.
- `scripts/kilimanjaro-manifest.mjs` — a manifest that measures its own numbers instead of restating typed ones.

### Two factories, named apart

`adapterFactory` reads like the thing that talks to a model. It is not — it is the wire a compiled task travels over. I built the wrong shape on the first attempt. Each module's header now says which is which.

## The gate that was not guarding anything

`agent-mesh-activation-gate.mjs` decides whether the mesh may call a model provider at all, and nothing ever built its evidence input. An entry point with credentials configured would have called a provider with nothing between it and the money.

It is now evaluated on every tick and enforced:

| `permittedMode` | Workers run |
| --- | --- |
| `NO_PROVIDER_CALLS` | none |
| `SYNTHETIC_ONLY` | none |
| `ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY` | one, on a canary-ready provider |
| `BOUNDED_CLOUD_REHEARSAL` | all configured |

Evidence comes from two sources kept apart. **First-hand** facts the process checks itself are always computed and never overridable. **Attested** claims come from an operator JSON file. A file cannot upgrade a first-hand fact — otherwise the evidence file becomes a way to talk the gate into opening. There is a test for that attack.

No evidence file → `ARCHITECTURE_ONLY` / `NO_PROVIDER_CALLS`, the intended resting state. A file named but missing or malformed is a refusal, not a fallback.

Withheld workers exit 3, not 0. A scheduler running forever while its configured workers never run once is the silent failure this entry point exists to remove.

## Device-off cognition without an API key

`claude-code-sandbox` drives a local Claude Code CLI in an isolated sandbox. It needs no pricing evidence because the CLI reports its own usage and total cost — the number comes from the tool that spent it. When the CLI reports no cost the executor returns `UNCERTAIN` rather than zero.

**It is a local process, not free compute.** It consumes whatever account it is configured against. Nothing here makes any subscription unlimited or bypassable.

It requires an OS isolation receipt attesting an ephemeral filesystem, no mounted business credentials, no reachable production network, and Anthropic-only egress. The gate scores only the two API providers, so a sandbox worker is never eligible under `ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY` — unknown reads as not-permitted, asserted by a test.

## One reachable way to spend money

`agent-provider-execution.mjs` duplicates `agent-worker-runtime.mjs`'s reserve → invoke → commit transaction and had no importers. The runtime is canonical. The duplicate is marked SUPERSEDED and a test now fails if anything outside `tests/` imports it. Two reachable implementations of "spend money" is the shape that produces a double charge.

## Left open, deliberately

- **`durable-claude-engineering-executor.mjs` cannot be wired without new infrastructure.** Three of its five injectables — `createSandbox`, `destroySandbox`, `enterVerificationMode` — have no implementation anywhere in the repository. Every test stubs them. Recorded, not faked.
- **`agent-evolution-wave.mjs` is now wirable but left.** Wiring the mesh's self-modification path in the same pass that first made it runnable is not a safe ordering.
- **The 42 skips stay skipped.** All gated on `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, all concurrency proofs. PGlite is real PostgreSQL but serves one connection at a time; running them against it would report guarantees never exercised.
- **The mesh has never been observed doing real work.** Reachable is not proven-in-production, and nothing here claims it is.

## Why

PR #40's scheduler-safe worker tick scanned the global pending-result store with `limit: 1` and replayed the first record it saw before claiming new work. title: Fix the HTTP ingress: poll was broken, and receipts lost their provenance
head: a77cbb2fee0a00fdb8167b6ca3dcf86be59a1186
body:
The ingress had **never handled a real request.** Every test drove it with a fake client, so nothing had ever exercised the code that builds GitHub URLs or forwards a submit.

I ran it once against the real API. Two defects, immediately.

## 1. `poll` returned 400

The transport passes `state: 'OPEN'`. GitHub answers **422** for anything but lowercase:

```
OPEN   -> 422 {"message":"Validation Failed","errors":[{"value":"OPEN",...}]}
open   -> 200 []
```

**The operation ChatGPT uses to discover work at all was broken against the real API** — while the unit suite was green, because every fake accepted whatever it was handed.

Normalised at the client boundary, which is the layer that has to speak GitHub's dialect, rather than asking each caller to remember.

## 2. Receipt provenance was discarded in silence

Only `workerId`, `status` and `result` were forwarded. A caller that carefully supplied the rest got this:

| sent | filed |
|---|---|
| `sourceCommit: "deadbee"` | `"UNKNOWN"` |
| `confidence: "HIGH"` | `"UNKNOWN"` |
| `findings: [...]` | `[]` |
| `limitations: [...]` | `[]` |
| `duration: 1234` | `null` |

…and a **200 RECEIVED** in reply. Dropping evidence while reporting success is the worst failure this contract can have. Issue #65 captures it; #66 is the same request afterwards with every field intact.

## The fakes were the reason this hid

The tests now drive the **real client** through a fake `fetch`, and the fake **behaves like GitHub** — it returns 422 for a non-lowercase state, exactly as the API does.

A fake that says yes to everything isn't a test double, it's a way to keep a bug.

One new test exists for a failure mode worse than the 400: a validation error that becomes `200` with `count:0`, which reads as *"no work to do"* when the truth is *"the query was rejected"*. It pins that this fails loudly.

## Both tests verified by breaking the fix

A test that cannot fail is not protection, so I reverted each fix in turn:

```
revert lowercase fix  -> not ok 10 - poll asks GitHub for a lowercase state
revert provenance fix -> not ok 13 - submit forwards the provenance the caller sent
restored              -> 13 pass, 0 fail
```

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:syntax` | pass |
| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1195 tests, 1153 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| `tests/vercel-agent-relay.test.mjs` | 13/13 |
| live | #65 broken behaviour, #66 fixed, both closed |

## Still true

The ingress is **deployed nowhere.** This was driven over loopback against the real GitHub API, which exercises every line except the hosting. It does not become live until someone pastes credentials into Vercel — but it is now worth deploying, which it demonstrably wasn't an hour ago.

title: Stop the worker reporting a killed suite as a failure, or a lost result as work done
head: d154212c9e49b7009fb2f57d6bdcf408cfb2f68b
body:
Two defects, both the same kind: **a failure shaped like a success.**

## 1. A timed-out suite was reported as a failed one

`execFile` signals a timeout kill exactly like a non-zero exit. Nothing separated them, so a suite that never finished produced:

```
status/conf : FAILED / HIGH
test result : FAIL
truthTable  : {"deterministic":"FAILED"}
decision    : REPAIR
```

Every line is false. **The deterministic suite passes — 1191 tests, 0 failures.** It was killed, not failed. The receipt asserted a verification result it never obtained, at *high* confidence, and asked a reviewer to repair something that is fine.

That's the precise dishonesty the receipt contract exists to prevent, coming from the one producer nobody watches.

Now: `NOT_RUN`, `LOW`, `OWNER_REQUIRED`, and a limitation saying in plain words *"this is not evidence that the suite fails."*

### The first attempt at this fix didn't work

Worth recording rather than hiding. I tested `error.code === undefined`. Node sets it to **`null`** on a timeout kill — so the condition silently never matched and the bug shipped looking fixed. Issue #61 is the receipt it produced.

`killed === true` is the marker. I checked the real error object the second time instead of guessing again.

| | #61 (before) | #62 (after) |
|---|---|---|
| status / confidence | `FAILED` / `HIGH` | `FAILED` / `LOW` |
| test result | `FAIL` | `NOT_RUN` |
| truthTable | `FAILED` | `NOT_RUN` |
| decision | `REPAIR` | `OWNER_REQUIRED` |
| limitations | 2 | 3, including the explicit disclaimer |

## 2. A failed submit counted as handled work

`handled += 1` ran unconditionally. So a result that couldn't be filed:

- consumed a slot against `maxTasks` — the worker stopped early having accomplished nothing
- logged at normal level, as though the task were done

Meanwhile the lease lapses, the task strands, and **one of its three attempts is spent on work that completed and was thrown away.**

Now it logs `SUBMIT FAILED` at error level, counts nothing, and exits non-zero so a scheduler notices instead of recording a clean run. Proved on #63:

```
SUBMIT FAILED on #63: task-already-completed. The suite ran but its result
could not be filed; this attempt is lost and the task will strand.
done; handled 0 task(s), 1 submit failure(s).
exit code 1
```

Getting that scenario required care: an actively heartbeating worker can't lose its lease, so I used a short suite with the default 60s heartbeat — no renewal fires — and changed the task state mid-run.

## A correction

When I proposed this work I said a stale poll snapshot was the next bug. **It isn't.** `claimGithubRelayTask` re-reads the issue and its comments and refuses with `task-already-completed`, so the claim is the authority and the snapshot can't cause duplicate work. I checked before building anything, and found these two instead.

| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1191 tests, 1149 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| live | #61 old behaviour, #62 corrected, #63 submit loss |
| queue after | `IDLE`, 0 open |

title: Renew the lease while a suite runs, and stop when it is gone
head: 9706b87627b408d99d34bd8e1def86fe5d64c060
body:
## The gap

The worker **never heartbeated.** A suite runs for minutes; the lease is finite. Nothing renewed it.

So a slow machine or a longer suite lets the lease lapse mid-run, another worker takes the task, and this one finishes, tries to submit, and gets `lease-owner-mismatch` — every minute of work discarded, with no message anyone would think to go looking for.

It happens to fit today because `check:syntax` takes 16 seconds against a 1800-second lease. That's margin, not a design.

## What changed

Renews once a minute while a suite runs (`RELAY_HEARTBEAT_MS`). If a renewal is **refused**, it kills the child rather than spending the remaining minutes producing a result it cannot submit.

A transient network error is **not** treated as a lost lease — only an explicit refusal counts. The two aren't the same, and guessing wrong throws away good work.

## Both branches proved live

**Renewal** — `test:deterministic` (~2 min), 20-second interval, issue #57:

```
claimed #57 attempt 1/3
renewed the lease 5 time(s) during #57
#57 -> RECEIVED
```

**Abort** — and here the obvious test *couldn't work*, which is worth reading.

I had a rival worker submit a competing result 40 seconds into a run. It was **refused** with `lease-owner-mismatch` (issue #58) — because an actively heartbeating worker still holds a live lease. The feature had made its own failure scenario unreachable. Good news, but it left the abort branch unproven.

So I forced the state instead: wrote the result comment directly, which is what `resolveLease` actually reads to decide a task is COMPLETED (issue #59):

```
claimed #59 attempt 1/3
lease lost mid-run on #59: task-already-completed -- aborting
abandoning #59: lease lost to another worker mid-run. No result submitted.
done; handled 0 task(s).
```

Killed the child, submitted nothing, didn't overwrite the other owner's history.

## One more thing worth knowing

A task created and polled seconds later can be **invisible** — GitHub's label index lags issue creation. My first heartbeat run reported `0 task(s) visible` for an issue I'd just made.

Not a defect here: the next scheduled run picks it up. But it looks exactly like a packet parse failure, and it isn't one — I verified the packet parses fine and the same poll returned it a minute later. Recording it so the next person doesn't spend an hour debugging their own code.

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:syntax` | pass |
| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1191 tests, 1149 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| live renewal | #57, 5 renewals across a 2-minute suite |
| live theft attempt | #58, correctly refused |
| live abort | #59, detected, killed, submitted nothing |

title: Let the worker actually reach the recovery path, and emit a real receipt
head: c0e88a730a1f28ecc3f20b36a280261613bca920
body:
Two defects in the unattended worker. Both found by running it against a genuinely stranded task rather than by reading it.

## 1. The recovery path was unreachable

The worker filtered candidates on `!task.claimed`. But `claimed` means only *"the `agent-relay:claimed` label is present"* — and **that label stays on a task whose worker died holding the lease.**

So abandoned tasks were invisible to the one process able to rescue them. Lease recovery was shipped in #54, tested, documented — and could never once have run in production.

It now considers already-claimed tasks too and lets `claimGithubRelayTask` decide, since that function reads the real lease from the comments and is the only authority on whether one is live. Fresh work still goes first; recovery is what a worker does when there's nothing new.

**Verified end to end.** A task abandoned by `dead-worker`:

```
1 task(s) visible, 0 unclaimed, 1 already-claimed (checked for an abandoned lease)
recovered #55 -- previous holder dead-worker abandoned it, attempt 2/3
#55 -> RECEIVED
```

The identical run before this change reported `0 unclaimed` and exited.

## 2. The receipts were hollow

The worker filled in **none** of the fourteen mandated receipt fields. The only unattended producer in the system was emitting the weakest evidence in it — `sourceCommit: UNKNOWN`, `confidence: UNKNOWN`, no limitations. A receipt that cannot name the commit it describes is not evidence of anything.

It now resolves the commit once per run and reports real commands, tests, duration, findings and limitations. Actual receipt from #55:

```
sourceCommit  : "43445c2"
confidence    : "HIGH"
duration      : 16628
commands      : ["npm run check:syntax"]
tests         : npm run check:syntax -> PASS
limitations   : 2 recorded
fields        : 16
validates     : []          <- no reason codes
```

**Confidence is `HIGH` only when a suite actually ran to completion.** An unsupported objective produced no evidence at all, so claiming confidence in it would be exactly the dishonesty the receipt contract exists to prevent — those receipts report `LOW` and say the objective was not attempted.

## Worth noting

Defect 1 is a failure mode I should call out plainly: I shipped recovery in #54 with passing tests and a live proof, and it was still dead code in the only place it mattered. The tests exercised `claimGithubRelayTask` directly; nothing exercised *the worker choosing which tasks to offer it*. The proof used direct claim calls too. Both were green and both missed it.

What caught it was running the actual worker binary against a real stranded task — the same pattern that found every other real bug this session.

| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1191 tests, 1149 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |

title: Recover abandoned tasks visibly, and stop retrying the ones that keep killing workers
head: 921610ce988b601b225c9ad35e76c14d4b46515d
body:
## What was wrong

An expired lease was already claimable again — that's the recovery path and it's correct. Two things about how it worked weren't.

**It was silent.** A worker took over an abandoned task and the thread read as though the first attempt never happened. That's precisely the history someone debugging a repeatedly-failing task needs to see.

**It was unbounded.** A task that kills whatever picks it up got handed to worker after worker forever, burning one per cycle while the issue list showed healthy-looking activity — a crash loop wearing a queue as a costume.

## What changed

A takeover now announces itself in the comment and carries `recoveredFrom`/`lapsedAt` in the packet, and the claim returns `CLAIMED_RECOVERED` rather than plain `CLAIMED`.

Claims are capped — default 3, configurable — and refuse past it with `task-exceeded-max-attempts`.

**Ordering matters and is tested:** the cap is checked *after* the live-lease guard. Reversed, a task under its limit would let a second worker barge in on a lease that's still alive.

## Proved on real GitHub, not fixtures

Issue #52, three one-second leases stranding in sequence:

```
1st  CLAIMED            attempt 1
2nd  CLAIMED_RECOVERED  recovered from ghost-1, attempt 2
3rd  CLAIMED_RECOVERED  recovered from ghost-2, attempt 3
4th  REJECTED           task-exceeded-max-attempts
     "3 attempt(s) already recorded, limit 3. A task that strands
      repeatedly needs a person, not another worker."
```

## The proof found a follow-on gap worth as much as the feature

Capping attempts creates a *new* permanent state, and `relay-status` reported it identically to an ordinary stranded task — telling the reader to run another worker, **the one action that cannot possibly work.**

`EXHAUSTED` is now a distinct verdict outranking `STRANDED`:

```
verdict    : EXHAUSTED
  EXHAUSTED  #52 recovery-proof-...  3 attempts, last ghost-3 -- no worker will retry this

A task hit its attempt limit. Workers will refuse it now, so running
another one changes nothing. Read the claim history on the issue and
decide whether to fix the task, split it, or close it.
```

The worker likewise distinguishes `GIVING UP` from an ordinary skip — logging both as "skipped" hid the difference exactly when it mattered.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:syntax` | pass |
| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1191 tests, 1149 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| `tests/github-relay.test.mjs` | 33/33 |
| live recovery proof | issue #52 — recovery chain + cap, as above |
| live round trip, re-run after | issue #53, all 10 steps, both guards fire |

I re-ran the full round trip after changing the claim path specifically because this touches it — a regression there would break the bridge itself.

Issues #52 and #53 are closed with explanations of why they existed. No work ran under either; no external effect.

title: Make the relay say what it is doing
head: 2968f8939f9d54eee27998c3088008eea23bc3de
body:
## The gap

The GitHub issue list cannot answer *"is the relay working?"*

An issue labelled `agent-relay:claimed` looks **identical** whether a worker is mid-run or died an hour ago holding the lease. A queue with nothing running looks **identical** to a queue being actively worked. Those need opposite responses, and until now the only way to tell them apart was to read comment timestamps by hand.

## Four states that actually differ

| | |
|---|---|
| `IDLE` | Nothing to do. |
| `ACTIVE` | Work waiting or in flight, someone is on it. |
| `STALLED` | Work waiting, nothing running. **Not broken** — nobody is home. The easiest failure to mistake for a crash. |
| `STRANDED` | A worker claimed a task and vanished. The lease lapsed so the task is claimable again, but work may have been done and thrown away, and nothing announces that. |

`STRANDED` outranks `STALLED` deliberately: idle means nobody started; stranded means someone started and disappeared.

`summarizeRelayQueue()` is a **pure function** over issues, comments and `now` — testable without a network, and it can't drift from what the transport actually reports. `scripts/relay-status.mjs` is a thin read-only wrapper that **exits 1** on `STRANDED`/`STALLED`, so it can gate a check without anyone parsing output.

```
relay queue: mohammedwessam2007/uberbondd   2026-08-21T00:24:17Z
verdict    : STRANDED
open tasks : 1  (queued 0, claimed 0, lease-expired 1)
  STRANDED   #50 relay-status-proof-...  last held by worker-ghost, 1 attempt(s)

A worker claimed a task and never finished it. The lease has lapsed so the
task is claimable again, but any work it did was lost. Re-run a worker.
```

## Proved against real GitHub, and it found a bug

I opened issue #50 and claimed it with a **one-second lease** so it would strand immediately. Detection worked — and the run exposed a gap worth more than the feature itself:

> `STRANDED #50 ... last held by null`

`resolveLease()` was **discarding the claimant** once a lease expired. For a stranded task that is the single fact you need — *which worker vanished*. You'd have been told something was abandoned with nowhere to look.

`lastHolder` and `lapsedAt` are now preserved. `holder` deliberately stays `null`, because nobody holds an expired lease and existing callers branch on exactly that — so the new fields cannot change any current decision. There's a test pinning that distinction.

Issue #50 is closed with a comment explaining why it existed. No work ran under it; no external effect.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:syntax` | pass |
| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1184 tests, 1142 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| `tests/github-relay.test.mjs` | 26/26 |
| live check | STRANDED detected on real GitHub, exit 1; IDLE after cleanup, exit 0 |

The 8 new tests cover each verdict, the boundary where a running worker prevents `STALLED`, retry detection, the `holder`/`lastHolder` distinction, and a strictly zero effect ledger — reading a queue changes nothing.

title: Tell mechanical merge conflicts apart from real ones, automatically
head: 988c831add950913409675dc9b4c6df069ade551
body:
## Why

The same twenty-minute ritual kept repeating: throwaway worktree, merge main, stare at conflicts, work out whether they're real, run the suite, write it up. Three times this week — and **twice out of three the answer was "both sides appended to the same list."**

`git` already tells you *whether* a branch conflicts. What it can't tell you is whether the conflict **matters**. Those two cases look identical in a status output and need completely different responses:

| | |
|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL** | Both sides added in the same place. A union resolves it, nothing is lost. Nobody needs to think. |
| **NEEDS_HUMAN** | The sides changed the same thing to different values. One has to win, and only a person can say which. |

## The tool

`scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs` classifies every open PR in one command. **Read-only** — never pushes, never writes to a branch, removes every worktree it creates. Running the suite is opt-in (`--test`) because it's slow.

```
node scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs                 # classify all open PRs
node scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs --test          # also run the gate where merge is clean
node scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs --pr 37 --pr 40 # only these
node scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs --json          # machine-readable
```

## What it says about the queue right now

One command, not an afternoon:

```
#45 [draft] MECHANICAL   package.json  2 regions, 4 lines -- script-list (union)
#40 [draft] CLEAN
#7  [draft] NEEDS_HUMAN  src/store.mjs        5 regions, 194 lines -- divergent
                         src/job-handlers.mjs 1 region,  128 lines -- divergent
#5  [draft] NEEDS_HUMAN  src/store.mjs       11 regions, 201 lines -- divergent
                         + 9 other files
```

**PR #7's blocker is now concrete rather than vague.** Both sides evolved the *same schema in different directions* — the PR sits at `version: 9` with `sourceEvidence`/`opportunities`, main at `version: 6` with `providerEvents`/`leadLists`. That's a versioning decision with migration implications, not a merge. Worth knowing before anyone opens the file.

## Two bugs found by running it, not reading it

- A PR head pushed since the last fetch failed with a bare `invalid reference`, which reads like a broken PR rather than an unfetched ref. #45 reported `ERROR` until fixed; it's `MECHANICAL`.

title: Scan for secrets by type, not by name — unblocks PR #40's hidden failing test
head: 92c10737fc9375ed5b8faa7e5ce3ce93b43c8e93
body:
## The bug, third occurrence

This codebase counts compute in units it calls *tokens*. `maxTokens` on a task budget. `tokens` in receipt cost accounting. And now `coordination.tokenBudget` in the autonomy worker. All three match `SECRET_KEY = /token|secret|password|.../i`, so all three were rejected as credentials — legitimate payloads refused.

I fixed the first two by naming them as exceptions. That was treating the symptom. A fourth name was always going to show up, and it did.

## The fix

An authentication token is a **string**. A counter is a **number**.

```js
if (/token/i.test(key) && isComputeCount(item)) return false;
```

A token-shaped key holding a non-negative integer (or an explicitly unmeasured `null`) is a counter and passes, whatever it's called. A string under the same key still falls through to the scanner, so a real credential hidden under `tokenBudget` is caught exactly as before. The exemption is deliberately limited to `/token/i` — `password`, `apikey`, `secret` have no counter meaning and stay blocked whatever their value.

## One assertion changed, deliberately

`hasSecret({ accessToken: 1 })` was `true`, is now `false`. I'm calling that out rather than letting it slide past in a diff.

It's the intended trade. The integer `1` is not a usable credential, so rejecting it bought no safety, while the strict name-based reading cost three real false positives. What the scanner exists to prevent — a high-entropy string leaking into a public issue — is unaffected. The negative cases now pin that explicitly:

```js
hasSecret({ coordination: { tokenBudget: 'ghp_abcdefghijklmno' } })  // true
hasSecret({ cost: { tokens: 'Bearer abcdefghijkl' } })              // true
hasSecret({ cost: { tokens: -5 } })                                 // true
hasSecret({ cost: { tokens: 1.5 } })                                // true
hasSecret({ password: 1 })                                          // true
hasSecret({ clientSecret: 0 })                                      // true
```

## How it was found, which is the part worth reading

**PR #40 adds 22 test files and never touches `package.json`.** None of them are in `test:deterministic` or `check:syntax`. They have never run — not locally, not in CI, not once.

I ran them. `tests/openai-worker-roundtrip.test.mjs` was **failing on that branch**, and there was no way for anyone to find out. It fails at the branch tip on its own, so this is not something my earlier changes introduced — I checked that specifically before writing a line of fix.

With this change alone, PR #40's suite goes **313/314 → 314/314**.

## What this is

The bridge could already carry a task. What it could not do was let the other side **verify** what came back. A receipt that says `COMPLETED` and nothing else tells a reviewer nothing — not what commit ran, not what executed, not what the worker was unable to check.

Four commits, all relay-scoped.

## The changes

**`5995ba8` — receipts you can actually check.** The receipt contract goes from 6 fields to the full 14. Two matter most: `sourceCommit`, without which a receipt floats free of the code it describes, and `limitations`, without which a partially-blocked task reads as a clean pass. `validateRelayReceipt()` rejects missing fields, unrecognised confidence levels, and any receipt claiming a nonzero external effect. Adds `githubRelayTaskEnvelope()`, which derives status, lease, attempts and idempotency key from the issue itself rather than keeping a second copy of the truth to drift out of sync.

**`bf8b509` — one handoff document.** There were five documents describing the bridge, written at different times, disagreeing about what was live. That is worse than none: a reader believes whichever they open first. `docs/LIVE_BRIDGE_HANDOFF.md` is now canonical; the other five carry a banner pointing at it.

**`e6d5526` — the proof, as a script.** The bridge had been proven by a throwaway script that then vanished, so the claim could only be taken on faith. `scripts/github-relay-roundtrip.mjs` drives one task around the whole loop against the real GitHub API and exits non-zero if any guard fails to fire.

**`163c8c2` — capability graph.** The `github-relay-transport` entry now cites this wave's evidence instead of two-wave-old evidence. Its known limitations are unchanged.

`cost.tokens` (a compute-unit counter) and `externalEffects.credentialChanges` were tripping the secret scan on key name alone, **rejecting legitimate receipts**. That is the failure direction that quietly teaches people to route around a safety check.

The replay guard was probed with a deliberately thin payload — which schema validation rejected *before* the completion check ever ran. Green test, guard never reached. ## Outcome

The device-off path was **staged but had never run**. Running it surfaced two defects a green test suite could not, both of which would have made the "device-off" claim false in practice.

## Proven unattended — on a task this worker did not author

[Issue #32](https://github.com/mohammedwessam2007/uberbondd/issues/32) ("Verify Vercel relay ingress") was created by a **different agent** and handled end to end by `scripts/github-relay-worker.mjs` using only Bash and the environment credential — **no MCP tools, no human, no GitHub Actions, no Vercel**:

```
[github-relay-worker] authenticated as mohammedwessam2007 (via env proxy)
[github-relay-worker] 1 task(s) visible, 1 unclaimed, target=claude-code
[github-relay-worker] claimed #32 (chatgpt-vercel-relay-check-20260820)
[github-relay-worker] #32 -> RECEIVED
```

Issue #32 is now `closed` / `agent-relay:done` with a result receipt carrying a strictly-zero effect ledger and `decision: PROCEED`.

## Defect 1 — Node's `fetch` silently ignores `HTTPS_PROXY`

`curl` and `git` honour proxy env vars automatically; Node 22's global `fetch` does not unless `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`. In a proxied environment the **proxy is what carries the usable credential**, so every GitHub API call from the worker returned `401` while an identical `curl` returned `201`. Measured side by side rather than guessed:

```
curl via proxy                   -> 201
curl --noproxy '*'               -> 401
node fetch (default)             -> 401
node fetch NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1  -> 200
```

The worker now re-execs once with the flag when a proxy is configured, and is untouched on an ordinary host where none exists.

## Defect 2 — that failure would have stranded a real task

Claim happens **before** the work. A credential that fails on first write fails *after* the claim comment has already landed — leaving a genuine task locked under a lease held by an already-dead worker until it expires, unclaimable by anyone else.

Added a `GET /user` credential preflight that refuses to claim anything if it fails. One extra request removes that entire class of outage.

## `VERIFIED_LIVE` had to be added to the enum

`github-relay-transport` is promoted to `VERIFIED_LIVE` — and that status **did not exist** in `CAPABILITY_STATUSES` until now, because nothing in UberBond had ever earned it. Everything was either tested-but-never-run (`TEST_VERIFIED`) or run-but-unproven (`LIVE_UNPROVEN`).

A regression test guards it so it can't be handed out cheaply later: anything claiming `VERIFIED_LIVE` must cite an externally-addressable artifact — an issue number, a receipt, a deployment — not just prose.

## Still not proven, and the docs say so

- The hourly Routine that fires this worker has **not yet fired on its own schedule**. The worker is proven; the scheduler invoking it is not, until its first real firing.
- `.github/workflows/agent-relay-worker.yml` remains unexecuted while GitHub Actions is blocked on this account (green through 2026-07-17, then ~3–10s failures with 404 logs).

## Outcome

The relay was blocked on a deployed HTTP host that does not exist, and that was being treated as "no live bridge is possible." It wasn't. The mission's own Wave 5 listed a **GitHub-mediated task packet** as an available path, and GitHub is already a durable, authenticated, always-on store both ends can reach — no new host, no new spend, no new credential.

`src/github-relay.mjs` implements that transport, and **it has now carried a real task end to end on real infrastructure.**

## The live proof — issue #30

| Step | Real artifact |
|---|---|
| Producer opens a task | [issue #30](https://github.com/mohammedwessam2007/uberbondd/issues/30), label `agent-relay:task` |
| Packet compiled | same `compileAgentTask()` the HTTP relay uses |
| Worker polls + claims | claim comment `5348571058`, 1800s lease |
| Worker does real work | `npm run test:deterministic` → **1092 tests, 1050 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped, exit 0** |
| Worker returns receipt | result comment `5348593358` |
| Task closed | `agent-relay:done`, state `closed` |

No mock at any hop. Real issue, real comment ids, real timestamps, real measured numbers. The reviewer round-trip was then re-verified against the real comment bodies pulled back from GitHub: `resolveLease()` reports `HELD` during the work and `COMPLETED` after, and `parseResultComment()` recovers 1092/1050/0 intact.

## A real defect the live run found that no fixture could

Reading issue #30's body back returned it **HTML-escaped** — `"` arrived as `"` — so `JSON.parse` failed and the relay reported **zero claimable tasks while a perfectly valid task sat open on the repo.** A silent, total failure of the bridge, invisible to every unit test.

Worse, the escaping is **inconsistent between endpoints on the same client**: the issue *body* came back escaped, its *comments* came back raw. So a client author can't just decide "this API escapes" — the parser has to tolerate both on every read.

`extractFencedJson()` now tries raw first and falls back to single-pass entity decoding — single-pass specifically so a literal `&#34;` in content is never double-decoded into a quote. Regression-tested in both directions.

This is the clearest argument in the whole change for why "the tests pass" ≠ "it works."

## Same contract, different wire — not a second relay

This module imports `ZERO_EFFECTS`, `hasSecret()`, and `validResult()` from `src/cloud-agent-relay.mjs` rather than re-declaring them, and compiles packets with the same `compileAgentTask()`. The two transports cannot drift on what they consider safe. A result claiming any nonzero external effect is rejected identically on both.

## Staged for unattended, device-off operation

- **`scripts/github-relay-worker.mjs`** — runs **only** three allowlisted npm scripts (`check:syntax`, `test:deterministic`, `check`) and reports `UNSUPPORTED_OBJECTIVE` for anything else. It never executes free text from an issue body, because "anyone who can open an issue" must not mean "anyone who can run code in CI."
- **`.github/workflows/agent-relay-worker.yml`** — fires on `issues: opened/labeled` plus an hourly cron, concurrency-guarded so an event and a cron run can't both claim the same task, permissions limited to `issues:write` + `contents:read`. It cannot push, merge, deploy, or reach any other secret.

## Honest status: LIVE_UNPROVEN, not VERIFIED_LIVE

The one live run was driven by an interactive session acting as the worker. The unattended path is written and syntax-checked but has **never executed**, because GitHub Actions on this account is failing at the infrastructure level: CI ran clean and green through **2026-07-17**, then every run from commit `fe51c3c` onward completes in ~3–10s with job logs returning **HTTP 404**, across PRs #26/#28/#29 and the `main` merge. Jobs are dying before any step runs. That dates it to an Actions billing/quota lapse, not to the code — owner fix is GitHub → Settings → Billing.

## Honest limitation, stated in the module, the capability graph, and the docs

GitHub labels and comments are **not** database row locks. Two workers claiming in the same instant can both believe they hold the lease. `resolveLease()` resolves that deterministically after the fact (earliest server-assigned comment id wins, same answer regardless of asker or comment order) but cannot prevent duplicated work that already happened. Fine for a handful of owner-initiated tasks and one worker; unacceptable at high concurrency. `cloud-agent-relay.mjs` — with real `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` proven against a real PostgreSQL server — stays the transport to promote the moment a real host exists.

## Explicitly not done / not claimed

No deployed HTTP relay host. No ChatGPT connector configured. No messages sent, no spend, no scraping, no credential or DNS change, no production deploy. **$0 verified revenue, 0 paying customers, 0 accepted live deliveries — unchanged.**

- [x] Real end-to-end live run against real GitHub infrastructure (issue #30)

title: OMNIA V9 P2: canonical constitution binding
head: 059e5cf290b084ed655d2932e60a690970f0bbbd
body:
## Purpose

Stacked on P1 (#9). P2 replaces placeholder constitution hashes with a deterministic binding to UberBond's actual normative source documents, without pretending Markdown is executable policy.

## Reconciliation finding

The V9 research initially emphasized Core Data Model + Decision Engine + Learning Engine. Direct repository inspection showed that this source set is incomplete because the Decision and Learning engines normatively consume the Knowledge Graph, while the Core Data Model preserves the graph/decision/learning semantics as companion specifications.

P2 therefore binds exactly four sources:

1. `docs/constitution/knowledge-graph-v1.md`
2. `docs/constitution/decision-engine-v1.md`
3. `docs/constitution/learning-engine-v1.md`
4. `docs/constitution/core-data-model-v1.md`

Expected: Version `1.0.0`, effective `2026-07-14`.

## What P2 implements

- explicit source manifest with roles, paths, metadata, dependencies, normative anchors and source-anchored precedence rules
- deterministic exact-byte SHA-256 binding of each source
- fail-closed title/version/effective-date/anchor checks
- duplicate role/path rejection
- missing required dependency => `INCOMPLETE`
- normative dependency cycle => `CANONICAL_CONFLICT`
- unexpected constitutional role => conflict rather than silent expansion
- deterministic source-set + constitution digests independent of input map order
- one-byte source change changes the constitution digest
- precedence accepted only when the literal rule is present in the named source
- graded `verify-v9-p2`: `P2_CONSTITUTION_BOUND`, `INCOMPLETE`, `CANONICAL_CONFLICT`, or `FAIL`
- P2 tests wired into normal deterministic checks

## Explicit precedence bound from the real documents

- non-waivable Decision Engine gates override conflicting Learning Engine proposals
- Knowledge Graph priors may guide inspection but cannot by themselves create findings, recommendations, outreach claims or prices
- Core Data Model canonical semantics prohibit competing local meanings in products/APIs/agents/databases

No additional precedence is invented by AI merely because it sounds sensible.

## Verification truth

- **16/16 P2 binder/adversarial tests pass locally** on synthetic fixtures exercising the exact binder.
- Connected GitHub repository searches independently confirmed the critical literal Decision/Learning anchors used in the manifest.
- The exact-byte verifier over the four real repository files is implemented but has not executed in this sandbox because the repository is connector-only here and direct GitHub network cloning/resolution is unavailable.
- GitHub Actions is also currently prevented from starting runners by the account billing lock.
- Therefore this PR deliberately does **not** publish or hand-invent a real `constitutionDigest` and does not claim `P2_CONSTITUTION_BOUND` yet.

## Non-claims / P3 gates

- exact source binding is not semantic proof that every sentence of four long Markdown documents is contradiction-free
- Markdown is not executable policy
- Cedar or another policy engine should execute only a traceable projection of selected deterministic rules
- the policy bundle must bind exact policy source + schema + evaluator/runtime/build version
- owner sovereignty is not yet rooted in a separately signed owner-governance trust object

> V9 may execute only a traceable projection of law. The law itself remains the exact versioned normative source set, and any missing, changed, conflicting or unanchored source fails closed.

title: OMNIA V9 P1: persistent proof and atomic authority reservation
head: ef57368456de5ce1160626c1366d08fe261b1cb3
body:
## Purpose

Stacked on P0 (#8). P1 turns V9 authority from an in-memory decision into a persistent, budgeted, idempotent database reservation without touching production side effects.

## What P1 implements

- migration `005_omnia_v9_proof_store.sql`
- persistent proof objects for intents, owner approvals, evidence, authorization decisions and execution receipts
- proof-object re-canonicalization/re-hashing before persistence
- type-specific identity binding and tenant binding so signed/content-bound objects cannot be aliased across IDs or tenants
- target-resolved, tenant-bound revocation records
- database-owned approval use/cost counters
- idempotent authority reservations bound to exact stored intent digest + approval + tenant
- reservation-time resolution and verification of the exact stored `ActionIntent`
- reservation-time cryptographic re-verification of the persisted owner approval
- reservation-time re-evaluation of approval scope against the exact stored intent and locked usage row
- caller cost/blast/idempotency must match the content-bound intent; one intent reserves exactly one use in P1
- revoked action intents cannot reserve authority
- transaction flow that locks usage, enforces signed limits/scope, consumes budget, and marks authority `RESERVED`
- duplicate identical reservations do not double-consume authority
- same idempotency key cannot represent a different intent/approval/tenant
- `RELEASED` refunds reserved budget once; `COMMITTED` and `UNCERTAIN` retain consumption
- `persistAndReserveAdmission()` requires both P0 `ALLOW` and successful database authority reservation before `executable=true`
- graded `verify-v9-p1` command: `P1_DATABASE_VERIFIED`, `INCOMPLETE`, or `FAIL`
- migration `005` and the P1 suite are wired into the repository's normal deterministic/schema checks

## Test contract

The branch contains **20 materially distinct PGlite integration tests** covering migration, content re-hashing, identity/tenant binding, unsupported proof types, cryptographically forged approvals, invented/unstored intents, independent reservation-time scope checking, parameter/intention mismatch, single-use intent semantics, idempotency, persistent `maxUses`/cost limits, expiry, approval and intent revocation, release/commit semantics and end-to-end persistent admission.

### Current verification truth

- P0 remains **44/44 passing locally**.
- The local sandbox cannot import `@electric-sql/pglite` and its restricted package mirror cannot install it, so the P1 verifier correctly classifies database verification as **INCOMPLETE**, not PASS.
- GitHub Actions is currently prevented from starting runners by the repository/account billing lock; previous jobs had no runner and executed no code.
- Therefore this PR deliberately does **not** claim database verification yet.
- A true multi-connection PostgreSQL race test is still required before any production authority claim; PGlite's embedded single connection is not sufficient evidence for that race.

## Red-team repairs made before and after opening this PR

1. Persistence originally risked treating stored approval limits as authority; reservation now cryptographically re-verifies the exact signed approval every time.
2. A signed object could have been aliased under a different database ID; type-specific identity binding now rejects that.
3. Database tenant metadata could diverge from the content tenant; P1 now rejects that binding mismatch.
4. Persistence originally checked a declared digest but did not recompute it from stored content; every supported P1 proof object is now re-hashed before insertion.
5. Revocation now resolves the target object and enforces tenant ownership instead of accepting an arbitrary target ID.
6. Future proof-object classes without a registered digest algorithm are rejected rather than silently trusted.
7. Reservation originally accepted an arbitrary intent digest and trusted prior in-memory scope evaluation; it now resolves and verifies the stored intent, checks intent revocation, and re-runs approval scope inside the transaction against locked usage.
8. Caller-supplied cost/blast/idempotency could diverge from the intent; reservation now rejects divergence and permits one use per intent.

## Non-claims / next gates

P1 is not production-authoritative and introduces no live send/provider/deployment behavior.

Still required before consequence:

- run P1 DB tests in a valid dependency environment and then a real multi-connection PostgreSQL race test
- database-role/trigger hardening against direct SQL proof mutation
- resolved/authorized proof for revocation itself
- canonical constitution reconciliation/digest
- Cedar-backed policy bundle with exact evaluator/bundle digest binding
- typed resources instead of string-prefix scope
- resolvable attestations behind verification labels
- final-admission TOCTOU recheck after the existing outbound reservation and immediately before provider effect
- signed execution receipts and formal/mutation/fuzz/concurrency gates

> A digest is not authority. Stored approval is not spendable authority. Authority exists only when the exact stored intent and exact signed approval are freshly re-verified, unrevoked, in scope, and atomically reserved against database-owned usage.

## Purpose

Turn the V9 research verdict into executable software without changing production behavior.

- kill-state and intent-revocation dominance
- fail-closed policy adapter: missing/throwing policy authorizer => `DENY`
- consequential `ALLOW` requires versioned policy plus policy/constitution digests
- content-bound `ExecutionReceipt` creation plus independent verification
- shadow outbound adapter proving legacy `campaign.approved = true` is not sufficient authority and refusing to fabricate external evidence when no external URL exists

- V9 tests wired into the existing deterministic check suite

- **44/44 tests pass**
- **0 failures, 0 skipped**
- syntax checks pass for all V9 files
- verifier status: `P0_KERNEL_VERIFIED`

The adversarial suite covers closed-schema bypasses, unknown effect classes, digest tampering/format, expired/revoked/future/malformed approvals, invalid signatures, synthetic-vs-external evidence, fabricated external URLs, unknown evidence claims/lifecycle states, future-dated evidence, cross-tenant evidence, kill state, missing/throwing policy/evidence resolvers, missing policy/constitution digests, scope attenuation, use/cost budgets, malformed usage, `NaN`, receipt binding/tampering, legacy boolean authority, malformed timestamps, unresolved evidence, cyclic canonicalization and non-plain objects.

The verifier/review process already caught and forced repairs for seven real fail-closed weaknesses during P0 construction:

1. non-finite numeric input could throw instead of returning controlled denial;
2. malformed timestamps could become `NaN` comparisons;

4. callers could assert `effectKnown` instead of using a closed effect ontology;
5. consequential `ALLOW` did not require policy/constitution digests;
6. receipt creation lacked independent schema/time/cost verification;
7. canonicalization admitted more JavaScript object shapes than a signing boundary should.

This is **not final V9** and **not production-authoritative**.

Not yet implemented:

- canonical reconciliation/digest of the existing UberBond Core Data Model + Decision Engine + Learning Engine
- Cedar-backed production policy adapter and cryptographic binding of `policyDigest` to the exact evaluator/bundle
- persistent proof DAG / revocation / authorization / receipt storage
- PostgreSQL atomic consumption of bounded approval authority under concurrency

## Design law

> Intelligence may propose. Only resolved authority + resolved evidence + deterministic policy may admit consequence.

policy decisions, experiments, message variants, owner gates, deterministic scoring) on top of the
repo's existing PostgreSQL/JSON store, durable queue, and outbound-safety infrastructure, then

### Second-pass hardening (this update, commit `27cd700`)

Fixes seven further defects a follow-up audit found in the first repair pass (commit `f2f621d`):

- **Atomic evidence resolution**: the previous catch-a-conflict-then-query pattern is unsafe on
  Postgres (a failed statement aborts the rest of the transaction, so the recovery query never
  ran). Replaced with `store.mjs#findOrCreate` — a single atomic
  `INSERT...ON CONFLICT...RETURNING`. Proven with a real-Postgres test where two distinct
  opportunities, imported *concurrently*, correctly share one evidence row.
- **Gate/variant readiness linkage**: owner gates and message variants now require the linked

- **Readiness gates restored + full provenance**: `tenOfTenReadiness` restores the true original 14
  gates (the first pass had wrongly replaced three with unrelated technical ones) and adds the five
  gates named as missing (revenue attribution, accepted paid delivery, suppression testing,
  kill-switch testing, incident recovery). Every gate now requires full evidence provenance
  (evidenceRef/source/measurementWindow/timestamp), not a bare value.
- **Real content hashing**: `content_hash` is computed from real evidence content, not `signalKey`
  or the record id; `signalKey` is now its own column (migration 007). A fresher re-crawl always

- **Currency-safe owner gates**: now require `currency === 'USD'` outright (no FX-conversion source
  exists in this version) — raw cents from another currency can no longer satisfy the threshold.
- **Truly zero-write preview**: preview mode no longer writes even its own audit trail.

## Summary

Adds a bounded, resumable, **inbound-only** shadow autonomy cycle (`src/autonomy-cycle.mjs`): it reads Gmail (only when explicitly enabled), classifies incoming mail (bounce/complaint/unsubscribe/out-of-office/reply/unknown), suppresses future contact when warranted, records a bounded owner notification for ambiguous/positive replies, and writes a strict count-only, PII-redacted digest.

- **No reachable Gmail send capability.** `src/gmail-inbound.mjs` has `gmail.readonly` scope only, no `sendEmail` export, and is frozen against mutation. `autonomy-cycle.mjs` never imports `gmail.mjs`, `Pipeline`, `RevenueEngine`, `job-handlers.mjs`, or `queue.mjs` — proven by tests that read the actual source/export list, not just by not calling them.
- **No outbound or follow-up processing.** Those stages were removed from the design entirely rather than gated, since a prior (separately reviewed and rejected) version of this feature was found to still be exercising outbound capability even through a "test provider only" path.
- **Database-enforced singleton** for the active cycle, with compare-and-swap checkpointing — proven against two genuinely separate PostgreSQL connections, plus a real `SIGKILL` sent to an actual child process mid-stage, followed by real lease-expiry and resume from a fresh process.
- **Bounded everything**: pagination, MIME parsing depth/part-count/size, retries, per-stage and total cycle runtime.
- **No scheduled activation added.** No GitHub Actions workflow/cron exists for this — deliberately not built, which is a stronger guarantee than build-and-disable.

Full detail — including what was deliberately left out of scope (discovery/payment stages, live-Gmail-account testing, a full 164-case red-team matrix) — is in the six reports under `.claude/uberbond-continuity/release/` in this branch (not part of the diff itself; local continuity artifacts).
